import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Outer billiards

This file states two open problems about polygonal outer billiards in the Euclidean plane.

*Reference:*
- [Wikipedia, Outer billiard: Open problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_billiard%23open_problems)
-/

open MeasureTheory Set
open scoped EuclideanGeometry

namespace OuterBilliard

/-- The signed area form of the ordered pair of vectors `u`, `v` in the standard orientation of
`ℝ²`. In particular, `v` is on the closed right side of `u` when this value is nonpositive. -/
def signedArea (u v : ℝ²) : ℝ :=
  u 0 * v 1 - u 1 * v 0

/-- The closed polygonal table determined by its vertices. -/
def polygonTable {n : ℕ} (p : Fin n → ℝ²) : Set ℝ² :=
  convexHull ℝ (range p)

/-- A vertex `v` is the right-hand support vertex seen from `x` if it is a vertex of the polygon
and every vertex of the polygon is in the closed right half-plane of the ray from `x` through
`v`. -/
def IsRightSupportVertex {n : ℕ} (p : Fin n → ℝ²) (x v : ℝ²) : Prop :=
  v ∈ range p ∧ ∀ i, signedArea (v - x) (p i - v) ≤ 0

/-- One step of the polygonal outer-billiard map. It is defined exactly when there is a unique
right-hand support vertex, and then reflects the point through that vertex. Thus points whose
support line contains a side of the polygon have no step. -/
def IsStep {n : ℕ} (p : Fin n → ℝ²) (x y : ℝ²) : Prop :=
  ∃ v, IsRightSupportVertex p x v ∧
    (∀ w, IsRightSupportVertex p x w → w = v) ∧ y = 2 • v - x

/-- A well-defined (forward and backward) outer-billiard orbit is a bi-infinite sequence in which
every consecutive pair is related by an outer-billiard step. -/
def IsOrbit {n : ℕ} (p : Fin n → ℝ²) (z : ℤ → ℝ²) : Prop :=
  ∀ k, IsStep p (z k) (z (k + 1))

/-- An ordered vertex tuple is a regular polygon if it is a nondegenerate convex polygon with at
least three vertices and cyclic shifts preserve every distance between vertices. -/
def IsRegularPolygon {n : ℕ} (p : Fin n → ℝ²) : Prop :=
  3 ≤ n ∧ EuclideanGeometry.IsConvexPolygon p ∧
    ∀ i j k, dist (p i) (p j) = dist (p (i + k)) (p (j + k))

/-- For every `n ≥ 4`, Lebesgue-almost every ordered vertex tuple in `(ℝ²)ⁿ` which forms a
nondegenerate convex `n`-gon has an exterior point with a well-defined bi-infinite
outer-billiard orbit that is not contained in any bounded subset of `ℝ²`. The restriction
`n ≥ 4` excludes triangles, for which all outer-billiard orbits are bounded. -/
@[category research open, AMS 37]
theorem parts.i :
    ∀ n : ℕ, 4 ≤ n →
      ∀ᵐ p : Fin n → ℝ² ∂volume,
        EuclideanGeometry.IsConvexPolygon p →
          ∃ x z, x ∉ polygonTable p ∧ z 0 = x ∧ IsOrbit p z ∧
            ¬ Bornology.IsBounded (range z) := by
  sorry

/-- For every regular polygon with at least three vertices, Lebesgue-almost every point outside
the polygonal table has a well-defined bi-infinite outer-billiard orbit which is periodic. In
other words, the set of exterior points whose orbit is undefined or nonperiodic has measure
zero. -/
@[category research open, AMS 37]
theorem parts.ii :
    ∀ ⦃n : ℕ⦄ (p : Fin n → ℝ²), IsRegularPolygon p →
      ∀ᵐ x : ℝ² ∂volume, x ∉ polygonTable p →
        ∃ z : ℤ → ℝ², z 0 = x ∧ IsOrbit p z ∧
          ∃ m : ℕ, 0 < m ∧ Function.Periodic z (m : ℤ) := by
  sorry

end OuterBilliard
modeling_decisions: A polygon is parametrized by an ordered tuple `p : Fin n → ℝ²`; its closed table is `convexHull ℝ (Set.range p)`, and nondegenerate convexity uses the repository's `EuclideanGeometry.IsConvexPolygon`.

For part i, “almost every convex polygon” means Lebesgue-a.e. tuple in the ambient space `(Fin n → ℝ²)`, conditionally on that tuple forming a convex polygon. The conjecture is restricted to every `n ≥ 4`, explicitly excluding triangles as directed by the decomposition.

The outer-billiard map is modeled as a partial relation rather than a total function: a step exists only when the right-hand support vertex is unique, and its value is central reflection through that vertex. This leaves points on extensions of polygon sides undefined rather than assigning arbitrary values.

A well-defined orbit is represented by a bi-infinite sequence indexed by `ℤ`, matching the article's use of both the outer-billiard map and its inverse. Unboundedness means the sequence's range is not a bounded set.

A regular polygon is defined intrinsically as a nondegenerate convex tuple with at least three vertices for which every cyclic shift preserves all pairwise vertex distances. This includes arbitrary translations, rotations, reflections, and scales of regular polygons while excluding star orderings via convexity.

For part ii, the implication inside the Lebesgue-a.e. quantifier makes the exceptional set precisely the exterior points lacking a well-defined periodic orbit; periodicity is expressed by a strictly positive natural period cast to `ℤ`.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Outer billiards

Let $P$ be a compact convex set in the plane. Given a point $x_0$ outside $P$, the
*outer billiards map* sends $x_0$ to the point $x_1$ such that the segment from $x_0$ to $x_1$
is tangent to $P$ at its midpoint and $P$ lies to the right of the ray from $x_0$ through $x_1$.
Equivalently, $x_1$ is the reflection of $x_0$ through the right-hand support point of $P$ as
seen from $x_0$. When $P$ is a polygon the map is undefined at the points whose right-hand
support line contains a side of $P$; these points lie on finitely many lines, and almost every
point has a well-defined orbit.

An *orbit* is a two-sided sequence $\dots, x_{-1}, x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots$ in which every point is
the image of the previous one under the outer billiards map. An orbit is *periodic* if it
repeats, and *bounded* if some bounded region of the plane contains it.

The Wikipedia list of unsolved problems in mathematics lists "many problems concerning an
outer billiard, for example showing that outer billiards relative to almost every convex
polygon have unbounded orbits". This file states this problem and the second problem from the
open-problems section of the Wikipedia article on outer billiards: outer billiards relative to
a regular polygon has almost every orbit periodic.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, *Outer billiard*, Open questions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_billiard%23open_problems)
- [Wikipedia, *List of unsolved problems in mathematics*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [Sch07] R. E. Schwartz, *Unbounded orbits for outer billiards I*, J. Mod. Dyn. 1 (2007),
  371–424. [arXiv:math/0702073](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0702073)
- [Tab07] S. Tabachnikov, *A proof of Culter's theorem on the existence of periodic orbits in
  polygonal outer billiards*, Geom. Dedicata 129 (2007), 83–87.
  [arXiv:0706.1003](https://arxiv.org/abs/0706.1003)
- [Tab95] S. Tabachnikov, *Billiards*, Panoramas et Synthèses 1, Soc. Math. France, 1995.
-/

open EuclideanGeometry MeasureTheory Real

namespace OuterBilliard

/--
`IsOuterBilliardStep P x y` says that `y` is the image of `x` under the outer billiards map of
the convex table `P`: the point `x` lies outside `P`, and there is a point `v ∈ P` (the
right-hand support point of `P` as seen from `x`) which is the midpoint of the segment from `x`
to `y` and such that every other point of `P` lies strictly to the right of the ray from `x`
through `v`.

Here `∡ v x z` is the oriented angle at `x` from `v` to `z`; its sign is `-1` exactly when `z`
lies strictly clockwise of (to the right of) the ray from `x` through `v`.

If no such `v` exists (for a polygon `P`, this happens exactly when the right-hand support line
from `x` contains a side of `P`), the outer billiards map is undefined at `x`, and there is no
`y` with `IsOuterBilliardStep P x y`.
-/
def IsOuterBilliardStep (P : Set ℝ²) (x y : ℝ²) : Prop :=
  x ∉ P ∧ ∃ v ∈ P, midpoint ℝ x y = v ∧ ∀ z ∈ P, z ≠ v → (∡ v x z).sign = -1

/--
`IsOuterBilliardOrbit P o` says that the two-sided sequence `o : ℤ → ℝ²` is a well-defined
orbit of the outer billiards map of `P`: for every `n`, the point `o (n + 1)` is the image of
`o n`. A point `x` has a well-defined orbit exactly when there is such an `o` with `o 0 = x`.
-/
def IsOuterBilliardOrbit (P : Set ℝ²) (o : ℤ → ℝ²) : Prop :=
  ∀ n, IsOuterBilliardStep P (o n) (o (n + 1))

/--
The solid regular `n`-gon with centre `c` and circumradius `r`, with one vertex in the direction
`θ`: the convex hull of the points `c + r (cos (θ + 2πk/n), sin (θ + 2πk/n))` for
`k = 0, …, n - 1`.
-/
noncomputable def regularPolygon (n : ℕ) (c : ℝ²) (r θ : ℝ) : Set ℝ² :=
  convexHull ℝ (Set.range fun k : Fin n =>
    c + r • !₂[cos (θ + 2 * π * k / n), sin (θ + 2 * π * k / n)])

/-- The outer billiards map is single-valued: a point has at most one image. -/
@[category API, AMS 37 52]
theorem IsOuterBilliardStep.unique {P : Set ℝ²} {x y y' : ℝ²}
    (h : IsOuterBilliardStep P x y) (h' : IsOuterBilliardStep P x y') : y = y' := by
  obtain ⟨-, v, hv, hmid, hright⟩ := h
  obtain ⟨-, v', hv', hmid', hright'⟩ := h'
  by_cases hvv : v = v'
  · rw [midpoint_eq_iff] at hmid hmid'
    rw [← hmid, ← hmid', hvv]
  · have h₁ := hright v' hv' (Ne.symm hvv)
    have h₂ := hright' v hv hvv
    rw [oangle_rev, Real.Angle.sign_neg, h₁] at h₂
    exact absurd h₂ (by decide)

/-- The vertices of `regularPolygon n c r θ` lie on the circle of radius `r` about `c`. -/
@[category test, AMS 51]
theorem dist_regularPolygon_vertex (n : ℕ) (c : ℝ²) (r θ : ℝ) (hr : 0 ≤ r) (k : Fin n) :
    dist (c + r • !₂[cos (θ + 2 * π * k / n), sin (θ + 2 * π * k / n)]) c = r := by
  rw [dist_eq_norm, add_sub_cancel_left, norm_smul, Real.norm_of_nonneg hr, EuclideanSpace.norm_eq]
  simp [Fin.sum_univ_two, sq_abs, cos_sq_add_sin_sq]

/--
**Outer billiards relative to almost every convex polygon has unbounded orbits.**

Fix $n \ge 4$. For Lebesgue-almost every $n$-tuple $p$ of points of the plane that forms a
(non-degenerate) convex $n$-gon, the outer billiards map of the polygon $P = \mathrm{conv}(p)$
has an unbounded orbit: some point outside $P$ has a well-defined two-sided orbit that is not
contained in any bounded region.

Triangles ($n = 3$) are excluded: every triangle is affinely equivalent to a rational polygon,
so all of its orbits are bounded (Vivaldi–Shaidenko, Kolodziej, Gutkin–Simanyi), and the
statement is false for $n = 3$. For $n = 4$, unbounded orbits are known for irrational kites
[Sch07], while all orbits are bounded for trapezoids (Genin), which form a null set of
quadrilaterals; the problem is open in general.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 37 52]
theorem outer_billiard.parts.i (n : ℕ) (hn : 4 ≤ n) :
    ∀ᵐ p : Fin n → ℝ², IsConvexPolygon p →
      ∃ o, IsOuterBilliardOrbit (convexHull ℝ (Set.range p)) o ∧
        ¬ Bornology.IsBounded (Set.range o) := by
  sorry

/--
**Outer billiards relative to a regular polygon has almost every orbit periodic.**

For every regular $n$-gon $P$ ($n \ge 3$), Lebesgue-almost every point $x$ outside $P$ has a
well-defined two-sided outer billiards orbit, and this orbit is periodic. Equivalently, the set
of points outside $P$ whose orbit is undefined or not periodic has measure zero.

The cases of the equilateral triangle and the square are trivial (all orbits are periodic),
and Tabachnikov settled the case of the regular pentagon [Tab95]; the problem is open in
general.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 37 52]
theorem outer_billiard.parts.ii (n : ℕ) (hn : 3 ≤ n) (c : ℝ²) (r θ : ℝ) (hr : 0 < r) :
    ∀ᵐ x : ℝ², x ∉ regularPolygon n c r θ →
      ∃ o, o 0 = x ∧ IsOuterBilliardOrbit (regularPolygon n c r θ) o ∧
        ∃ k : ℕ, 0 < k ∧ Function.Periodic o (k : ℤ) := by
  sorry

end OuterBilliard

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Outer billiards

Outer billiards is a dynamical system defined relative to a convex shape $P$ in the plane.
For a point $x$ outside $P$, the outer billiards map sends $x$ to the point $y$ such that the
segment from $x$ to $y$ is tangent to $P$ at its midpoint and $P$ lies to the right of the ray
from $x$ to $y$. Equivalently, $y$ is the reflection of $x$ through the point where the right
support line from $x$ touches $P$. When $P$ is a polygon, the map is undefined at the points $x$
whose right support line meets $P$ along an edge. The (two-sided) orbit of a point $x$ is the
sequence obtained by iterating the map and its inverse; it is well defined when every iterate is
defined, which is the case for almost every point.

An orbit is *bounded* if it is contained in some bounded region of the plane, and *unbounded*
otherwise. An orbit is *periodic* if it eventually repeats. Since the outer billiards map is
injective where it is defined, a well-defined orbit eventually repeats if and only if it is
periodic in the usual sense.

The Wikipedia list of unsolved problems in mathematics records the open problems about outer
billiards, in particular whether outer billiards relative to almost every convex polygon has
unbounded orbits. The Wikipedia article on outer billiards also asks whether outer billiards
relative to a regular polygon has almost every orbit periodic.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, *Outer billiard*, Open questions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_billiard%23open_problems)
- [Wikipedia, *List of unsolved problems in mathematics*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [R. E. Schwartz, *Unbounded orbits for outer billiards I*](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0702073)
- [S. Tabachnikov, *A proof of Culter's theorem on the existence of periodic orbits in polygonal outer billiards*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0706.1003)
-/

open EuclideanGeometry MeasureTheory
open scoped Real

namespace OuterBilliard

/--
The points of `P` lying on the right support line from `x`: the points `v ∈ P` such that
all of `P` lies (weakly) to the right of the ray from `x` through `v`.

Here "to the right" is measured with the standard orientation of the plane: `p` lies to the right
of the ray from `x` through `v` when the signed area `areaForm (v - x) (p - x)` is nonpositive.
-/
def rightSupportPoints (P : Set ℝ²) (x : ℝ²) : Set ℝ² :=
  {v ∈ P | ∀ p ∈ P, positiveOrientation.areaForm (v - x) (p - x) ≤ 0}

/--
`Step P x y` means that `y` is the image of `x` under the outer billiards map relative to `P`:
`x` lies outside `P`, the right support line from `x` touches `P` in exactly one point `v`, and
`y` is the reflection of `x` through `v`. When the right support line from `x` meets `P` along a
segment, the outer billiards map is undefined at `x` and `Step P x y` fails for every `y`.
-/
def Step (P : Set ℝ²) (x y : ℝ²) : Prop :=
  x ∉ P ∧ ∃ v, rightSupportPoints P x = {v} ∧ y = Equiv.pointReflection v x

/--
`IsOrbit P o` means that the two-sided sequence `o : ℤ → ℝ²` is a well-defined outer
billiards orbit relative to `P`: for every `k`, the point `o (k + 1)` is the image of `o k`
under the outer billiards map. Such an orbit is determined by any one of its points.
-/
def IsOrbit (P : Set ℝ²) (o : ℤ → ℝ²) : Prop :=
  ∀ k, Step P (o k) (o (k + 1))

hull of the points `c + r • (cos (θ + 2πk/n), sin (θ + 2πk/n))` for `k = 0, …, n - 1`.
Every regular `n`-gon in the plane is of this form for some `c`, some `r > 0` and some `θ`.
-/
noncomputable def regularPolygon (n : ℕ) (c : ℝ²) (r θ : ℝ) : Set ℝ² :=
  convexHull ℝ (Set.range fun k : Fin n =>

theorem mem_rightSupportPoints_iff (P : Set ℝ²) (x v : ℝ²) :
    v ∈ rightSupportPoints P x ↔
      v ∈ P ∧ ∀ p ∈ P, (v 0 - x 0) * (p 1 - x 1) - (v 1 - x 1) * (p 0 - x 0) ≤ 0 := by
  have key : ∀ a b : ℝ², positiveOrientation.areaForm a b = a 0 * b 1 - a 1 * b 0 := by
    intro a b
    have h := triangle_area_eq_det a b 0
    simp only [triangle_area, vsub_eq_sub, sub_zero] at h
    simp [Matrix.det_fin_three] at h
    linarith
  simp only [rightSupportPoints, Set.mem_setOf_eq, key, WithLp.ofLp_sub, Pi.sub_apply]

theorem Step.unique {P : Set ℝ²} {x y y' : ℝ²} (h : Step P x y) (h' : Step P x y') :
    y = y' := by
  obtain ⟨-, v, hv, rfl⟩ := h
  obtain ⟨-, v', hv', rfl⟩ := h'
  rw [hv, Set.singleton_eq_singleton_iff] at hv'
  rw [hv']

/--

$(1, 3/2)$: walking from $(-1, 1/2)$ towards the vertex $(0, 1)$, the square lies on the right.
-/
@[category test, AMS 37 52]
theorem step_unitSquare :
    Step {p : ℝ² | p 0 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1 ∧ p 1 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1} !₂[-1, 1/2] !₂[1, 3/2] := by
  refine ⟨by simp, !₂[0, 1], ?_, ?_⟩
  · ext v
    rw [mem_rightSupportPoints_iff]
    simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq, Set.mem_Icc, Set.mem_singleton_iff]
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨⟨⟨h0, h1⟩, ⟨h2, h3⟩⟩, h⟩
      have := h !₂[0, 1] (by simp)
      simp at this
      ext i
      fin_cases i <;> simp <;> linarith
    · rintro rfl
      refine ⟨by simp, ?_⟩
      rintro p ⟨⟨h0, h1⟩, ⟨h2, h3⟩⟩
      simp
      linarith
  · ext i
    fin_cases i <;> simp [Equiv.pointReflection_apply]; norm_num

Relative to the unit square, the outer billiards map is undefined at the point $(-1, 1)$, which
lies on the extension of the top edge: the right support line from this point contains the whole
top edge.
-/

    ¬ Step {p : ℝ² | p 0 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1 ∧ p 1 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1} !₂[-1, 1] y := by
  rintro ⟨-, v, hv, -⟩
  have h₀ : !₂[(0 : ℝ), 1] ∈
      rightSupportPoints {p : ℝ² | p 0 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1 ∧ p 1 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1} !₂[-1, 1] := by
    rw [mem_rightSupportPoints_iff]
    refine ⟨by simp, ?_⟩
    rintro p ⟨⟨h0, h1⟩, ⟨h2, h3⟩⟩
    simp
    linarith
  have h₁ : !₂[(1 : ℝ), 1] ∈
      rightSupportPoints {p : ℝ² | p 0 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1 ∧ p 1 ∈ Set.Icc 0 1} !₂[-1, 1] := by
    rw [mem_rightSupportPoints_iff]
    refine ⟨by simp, ?_⟩
    rintro p ⟨⟨h0, h1⟩, ⟨h2, h3⟩⟩
    simp
    linarith
  rw [hv, Set.mem_singleton_iff] at h₀ h₁
  have := congrArg (· 0) (h₀.trans h₁.symm)

**Unbounded orbits for almost every convex polygon.**
Outer billiards relative to almost every convex polygon has unbounded orbits.

Precisely: for every $n \ge 4$ and Lebesgue almost every $n$-tuple of points
$(p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}) \in (\mathbb{R}^2)^n$ that are the vertices, in cyclic order, of a

tuples does not affect the meaning of "almost every".

kite) has unbounded orbits; these form a null set of quadrilaterals, so the problem is open.

@[category research open, AMS 37 52]
theorem outer_billiard.parts.i (n : ℕ) (hn : 4 ≤ n) :
    ∀ᵐ p : Fin n → ℝ², IsConvexPolygon p →
      ∃ o, IsOrbit (convexHull ℝ (Set.range p)) o ∧ ¬ Bornology.IsBounded (Set.range o) := by
  sorry

**Almost every orbit is periodic for regular polygons.**
Outer billiards relative to a regular polygon has almost every orbit periodic.

Precisely: for every regular $n$-gon $P$ (with $n \ge 3$), Lebesgue almost every point $x$ of

orbit is periodic.

regular pentagon ($n = 5$). These are the only cases known.

    ∀ᵐ x : ℝ², x ∉ regularPolygon n c r θ →
      ∃ o, IsOrbit (regularPolygon n c r θ) o ∧ o 0 = x ∧
        ∃ m : ℤ, 0 < m ∧ Function.Periodic o m := by
  sorry

end OuterBilliard

/-!
# Outer billiards

This file states two open problems about polygonal outer billiards in the Euclidean plane.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, "Outer billiard: Open problems"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_billiard%23open_problems)
- [Wikipedia, "List of unsolved problems in mathematics"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)

open EuclideanGeometry MeasureTheory

open scoped EuclideanGeometry

namespace OuterBilliard

/-- The signed area form on two vectors in the oriented Euclidean plane. -/
def cross (a b : ℝ²) : ℝ := a 0 * b 1 - a 1 * b 0

/--
`OuterStep v x y` says that `y` is obtained from `x` by reflection in a vertex of the
polygon `v`, and that the oriented line from `x` to `y` has the polygon on its right.
It is a relation because at points on extensions of sides the supporting vertex can be ambiguous.
-/
def OuterStep {n : ℕ} (v : Fin n → ℝ²) (x y : ℝ²) : Prop :=
  ∃ i, y = 2 • v i - x ∧ ∀ j, cross (y - x) (v j - x) ≤ 0

/--
A bi-infinite outer-billiard orbit. The uniqueness clauses exclude every point where either
the forward or backward outer-billiard map is ambiguous.
-/
def IsWellDefinedOrbit {n : ℕ} (v : Fin n → ℝ²) (o : ℤ → ℝ²) : Prop :=
  ∀ k, OuterStep v (o k) (o (k + 1)) ∧
    (∃! y, OuterStep v (o k) y) ∧ (∃! x, OuterStep v x (o k))

/-- A point has a well-defined unbounded outer-billiard orbit. -/
def HasUnboundedOrbit {n : ℕ} (v : Fin n → ℝ²) (x : ℝ²) : Prop :=
  ∃ o : ℤ → ℝ², o 0 = x ∧ IsWellDefinedOrbit v o ∧ ¬ Bornology.IsBounded (Set.range o)

/-- A point has a well-defined periodic outer-billiard orbit. -/
def HasPeriodicOrbit {n : ℕ} (v : Fin n → ℝ²) (x : ℝ²) : Prop :=
  ∃ o : ℤ → ℝ², o 0 = x ∧ IsWellDefinedOrbit v o ∧
    ∃ m : ℕ, 0 < m ∧ o (m : ℤ) = x

/--
The vertices form a regular polygon: after a translation, rotation, and positive scaling they
are the equally spaced points on the unit circle, listed counterclockwise.
-/
def IsRegularPolygon {n : ℕ} (v : Fin n → ℝ²) : Prop :=
  ∃ (c : ℝ²) (r θ : ℝ), 0 < r ∧
    ∀ i, v i = c + ![r * Real.cos (θ + 2 * Real.pi * (i : ℝ) / n),
      r * Real.sin (θ + 2 * Real.pi * (i : ℝ) / n)]

/--
For every $n\ge 4$, Lebesgue-almost every non-degenerate convex $n$-gon has a point outside
it whose well-defined outer-billiard orbit is unbounded. Here polygons are cyclically ordered
vertex tuples, and "almost every" refers to Lebesgue measure on $(\mathbb{R}^2)^n$.

The restriction $n\ge 4$ is necessary because all outer-billiard orbits of triangles are
bounded.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 37]
theorem outer_billiard.parts.i :
    ∀ n : ℕ, 4 ≤ n →
      volume {v : Fin n → ℝ² | IsConvexPolygon v ∧
        ¬ ∃ x ∉ convexHull ℝ (Set.range v), HasUnboundedOrbit v x} = 0 := by
  sorry

/--
For every regular $n$-gon with $n\ge 3$, the set of exterior points whose outer-billiard
orbit is undefined or is not periodic has Lebesgue measure zero.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 37]
theorem outer_billiard.parts.ii :
    ∀ (n : ℕ) (v : Fin n → ℝ²), 3 ≤ n → IsRegularPolygon v →
      volume {x : ℝ² | x ∉ convexHull ℝ (Set.range v) ∧ ¬ HasPeriodicOrbit v x} = 0 := by
  sorry

end OuterBilliard
modeling_decisions: A polygon is represented by a cyclically ordered tuple `v : Fin n → ℝ²`, using the existing `EuclideanGeometry.IsConvexPolygon`; its closed polygonal region is `convexHull ℝ (Set.range v)`.

For part i, “almost every convex polygon” is interpreted for each fixed `n ≥ 4` as ambient Lebesgue measure zero for the bad cyclic vertex tuples in `(ℝ²)^n`. The lower bound excludes triangles, whose outer-billiard orbits are all bounded.

The outer-billiard step is modeled as reflection in a listed vertex, with every polygon vertex on the right of the oriented line from the old point to the new point. It is kept relational so side-extension singularities remain ambiguous.
A well-defined orbit is bi-infinite and requires unique forward and backward relational steps at every iterate, matching the article's definition using both the outer map and its inverse.
An unbounded orbit means that its range is not a bounded subset of the Euclidean plane.

A periodic orbit is a well-defined bi-infinite orbit returning to its initial point after some positive natural-number iterate. For an invertible well-defined orbit this matches the article's “eventually repeats.”

A regular polygon is parametrized by a center, a positive radius, and a phase, with equally spaced counterclockwise vertices. This covers every Euclidean regular polygon as a region; vertex labeling does not affect the outer-step relation.

For part ii, the exceptional set consists of points outside the closed convex hull that do not have a well-defined periodic orbit. Thus both undefined and nonperiodic exterior points are counted, as required.

  ∃ z : ℤ → ℝ², z 0 = x ∧ IsWellDefinedOrbit v z ∧
    ∃ p : ℕ, 0 < p ∧ ∀ k : ℤ, z (k + p) = z k

points on a circle of positive radius. -/

  IsConvexPolygon v ∧
    ∃ (c : ℝ²) (r θ : ℝ), 0 < r ∧
      range v = range fun i : Fin n ↦
        c + r • !₂[Real.cos (θ + 2 * Real.pi * (i : ℝ) / n),

It is non-degenerate when the tuple is injective, its convex hull has nonempty interior, and every listed vertex is outside the convex hull of the other listed vertices. The right outer step from `x` through vertex `v i` is reflection `2 • v i - x`; the determinant inequality says all vertices, hence their convex hull, lie on the right of the oriented line from `x` to its image.

An orbit is unbounded when the range of its integer-indexed bi-infinite trajectory is not a bounded set.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Outer billiards

Outer billiards is a dynamical system defined relative to a convex shape $P$ in the plane.
Given a point $x_0$ outside $P$, there is typically a unique point $x_1$ such that the segment
$x_0 x_1$ is tangent to $P$ at its midpoint and $P$ lies to the right of the ray from $x_0$
to $x_1$. The map $x_0 \mapsto x_1$ is the outer billiards map. The backwards map is defined
by replacing "right" by "left"; it is the inverse of the outer billiards map. The orbit of a
point is the two-sided sequence obtained by iterating the map and its inverse.

When $P$ is a polygon the map is undefined at the points $x_0$ whose right-hand support line
meets $P$ in a segment, so some points do not have a well-defined orbit. These points are
contained in a countable union of lines, so almost every point has a well-defined orbit.

The list entry on Wikipedia reads: "Many problems concerning an outer billiard, for example
showing that outer billiards relative to almost every convex polygon have unbounded orbits."
This file states this problem and the second open problem from the article
(almost every orbit relative to a regular polygon is periodic).

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Outer billiard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_billiard%23open_problems)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [R. E. Schwartz, *Unbounded orbits for outer billiards I*](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0702073)
- [S. Tabachnikov, *A proof of Culter's theorem on existence of periodic orbits in polygonal
  outer billiards*](https://arxiv.org/abs/0706.1003)
-/

open EuclideanGeometry MeasureTheory Real

namespace OuterBilliard

/--
`IsStep P x y` says that `y` is the image of `x` under the outer billiards map relative to the
shape `P ⊆ ℝ²`: `x ∉ P` and the segment from `x` to `y` is tangent to `P` at its midpoint,
with `P` lying to the right of the ray from `x` to `y`.

Formally, the midpoint of `x` and `y` is the *unique* point `v ∈ P` such that every point `p` of
`P` lies weakly to the right of the ray from `x` through `v`, i.e.
`positiveOrientation.areaForm (v - x) (p - x) ≤ 0`. Here `positiveOrientation.areaForm a b` is
the determinant `a 0 * b 1 - a 1 * b 0`, which is negative exactly when `b` points to the right
of `a`.

If the right-hand support line from `x` meets `P` in a segment (which happens for some points
when `P` is a polygon), then the set of such `v` is not a singleton, so no `y` satisfies
`IsStep P x y`: the outer billiards map is undefined at `x`.
-/
def IsStep (P : Set ℝ²) (x y : ℝ²) : Prop :=
  x ∉ P ∧
    {v ∈ P | ∀ p ∈ P, positiveOrientation.areaForm (v - x) (p - x) ≤ 0} = {midpoint ℝ x y}

/--
`IsOrbit P x` says that the two-sided sequence `x : ℤ → ℝ²` is a well-defined outer billiards
orbit relative to `P`: for every `k`, the point `x (k + 1)` is the image of `x k` under the
outer billiards map (equivalently, `x k` is the image of `x (k + 1)` under the backwards map).
A point `x₀ ∉ P` has a well-defined orbit exactly when there is such an `x` with `x 0 = x₀`.
-/
def IsOrbit (P : Set ℝ²) (x : ℤ → ℝ²) : Prop :=
  ∀ k, IsStep P (x k) (x (k + 1))

@[category API, AMS 37]
theorem IsStep.not_mem {P : Set ℝ²} {x y : ℝ²} (h : IsStep P x y) : x ∉ P :=
  h.1

/-- The point of tangency `midpoint ℝ x y` of an outer billiards step lies in `P`. -/
@[category API, AMS 37]
theorem IsStep.midpoint_mem {P : Set ℝ²} {x y : ℝ²} (h : IsStep P x y) :
    midpoint ℝ x y ∈ P := by
  have : midpoint ℝ x y ∈
      {v ∈ P | ∀ p ∈ P, positiveOrientation.areaForm (v - x) (p - x) ≤ 0} := by
    rw [h.2]
    exact Set.mem_singleton _
  exact this.1

/-- An outer billiards step moves the point. -/
@[category API, AMS 37]
theorem IsStep.ne {P : Set ℝ²} {x y : ℝ²} (h : IsStep P x y) : x ≠ y := by
  rintro rfl
  exact h.not_mem (by simpa using h.midpoint_mem)

/-- The outer billiards map is single-valued. -/
@[category API, AMS 37]
theorem IsStep.unique {P : Set ℝ²} {x y y' : ℝ²} (h : IsStep P x y) (h' : IsStep P x y') :
    y = y' := by
  have := Set.singleton_eq_singleton_iff.mp (h.2.symm.trans h'.2)
  rw [midpoint_eq_iff] at this
  rw [← this, ← midpoint_eq_iff]

/-- Relative to a single point `c`, the outer billiards map is the reflection through `c`. -/
@[category test, AMS 37]
theorem isStep_singleton {c x : ℝ²} (hx : x ≠ c) :
    IsStep {c} x (AffineEquiv.pointReflection ℝ c x) := by
  have hm : midpoint ℝ x (AffineEquiv.pointReflection ℝ c x) = c := midpoint_eq_iff.mpr rfl
  refine ⟨by simpa using hx, ?_⟩
  rw [hm]
  ext v
  simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq, Set.mem_singleton_iff, forall_eq]
  refine ⟨fun h ↦ h.1, ?_⟩
  rintro rfl
  exact ⟨rfl, le_of_eq (Orientation.areaForm_apply_self _ _)⟩

/--
The regular `n`-gon with centre `c`, circumradius `r` and a vertex in the direction `θ`:
the convex hull of the points `c + r • (cos (θ + 2πk/n), sin (θ + 2πk/n))` for `0 ≤ k < n`.
-/
def regularPolygon (n : ℕ) (c : ℝ²) (r θ : ℝ) : Set ℝ² :=
  convexHull ℝ
    (Set.range fun k : Fin n ↦
      c + r • !₂[cos (θ + 2 * π * k / n), sin (θ + 2 * π * k / n)])

/--
**Outer billiards relative to almost every convex polygon has unbounded orbits.**

For every $n \ge 4$ and Lebesgue-almost every $n$-tuple of points $p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}$ in
$\mathbb{R}^2$ that are the vertices (in cyclic order) of a non-degenerate convex $n$-gon $P$,
the outer billiards system relative to $P$ has an unbounded orbit: there is a point outside $P$
with a well-defined (two-sided) outer billiards orbit that is not contained in any bounded
region of the plane.

Triangles are excluded (`4 ≤ n`): every triangle is affinely equivalent to a rational polygon,
so by the theorem of Vivaldi–Shaidenko, Kołodziej and Gutkin–Simanyi all of its orbits are
bounded. Since the outer billiards system is affinely natural, the conclusion does not depend on
the chosen parametrization of convex $n$-gons up to Lebesgue null sets.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 37 52]
theorem outer_billiard.parts.i (n : ℕ) (hn : 4 ≤ n) :
    ∀ᵐ p : Fin n → ℝ², IsConvexPolygon p →
      ∃ x : ℤ → ℝ², IsOrbit (convexHull ℝ (Set.range p)) x ∧
        ¬ Bornology.IsBounded (Set.range x) := by
  sorry

/--
**Outer billiards relative to a regular polygon has almost every orbit periodic.**

For every regular $n$-gon $P$ ($n \ge 3$), Lebesgue-almost every point $x_0$ outside $P$ has a
well-defined (two-sided) outer billiards orbit relative to $P$, and this orbit is periodic.
Equivalently, the set of points outside $P$ whose orbit is undefined or not periodic has
Lebesgue measure zero.

The cases $n = 3$ and $n = 4$ are trivial (all well-defined orbits are periodic), and
Tabachnikov settled the case $n = 5$; all other cases are open.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 37 52]
theorem outer_billiard.parts.ii (n : ℕ) (hn : 3 ≤ n) (c : ℝ²) (r θ : ℝ) (hr : 0 < r) :
    ∀ᵐ x₀ : ℝ², x₀ ∉ regularPolygon n c r θ →
      ∃ x : ℤ → ℝ², x 0 = x₀ ∧ IsOrbit (regularPolygon n c r θ) x ∧
        ∃ m : ℤ, 0 < m ∧ Function.Periodic x m := by
  sorry

end OuterBilliard

modeling_decisions: Outer billiards map defined for a general set P ⊆ ℝ² via the right-hand support point: IsStep P x y iff x ∉ P and midpoint ℝ x y is the unique v ∈ P with ∀ p ∈ P, areaForm (v - x) (p - x) ≤ 0. The choice of 'right' vs 'left' only inverts the map and does not affect either conjecture.

'Orbit' is the two-sided orbit of the article (iterate the map and its inverse); 'well-defined orbit' means every forward and backward step is defined, encoded as IsOrbit P (x : ℤ → ℝ²). Slot (i) therefore asks for a point whose full two-sided orbit is defined and unbounded (this is what Schwartz proved for the Penrose kite). A weaker forward-only reading was considered and rejected as less faithful to the article's definition of orbit.

Slot (i): 'almost every convex polygon' is read as: for each n, Lebesgue-a.e. vertex tuple p : Fin n → ℝ² (product measure on (ℝ²)^n) satisfying IsConvexPolygon p (strictly convex n-gon in cyclic order); the polygon is convexHull ℝ (Set.range p). Restricting to tuples in convex position is necessary: otherwise a positive-measure set of tuples would yield triangles.

Slot (i): n ≥ 4 is imposed because every triangle is affinely rational, so all triangle orbits are bounded (Kołodziej, Gutkin–Simanyi), which would make the n = 3 case false; this follows the decomposition notes and is explained in the docstring.
Slot (i): 'unbounded orbit' = ¬ Bornology.IsBounded (Set.range x); 'has unbounded orbits' = existence of at least one such orbit.

Slot (ii): quantified over all regular n-gons (centre, circumradius r > 0, rotation) for all n ≥ 3 rather than a single normalized one; 'almost every orbit periodic' is rendered as ∀ᵐ x₀, x₀ ∉ P → ∃ orbit through x₀ that is periodic (∃ m : ℤ, 0 < m ∧ Function.Periodic x m).
